tl;dr at the bottom The most recent time I lived on minimum wage was just over 2 years ago. Actually it was for two years, but I quit that job two years ago . . . almost to the day come to think of it. I also had already bought a house, but made sure the house payment (when I bought it) was low enough to afford on minimum wage just in case I was stuck working for that little again. When I bought my house I was making minimum wage +tips, but the tips weren't reported by my employer so I got a mortgage with my only proof of income being full-time minimum wage, and I hadn't had that position for a year, so no tax forms showing claimed tips. Let's just say, it was when the real estate market was bad, so I got a good deal on the house, but shitty PMI because I didn't have much to put down, but that will be gone in a few months.

Anyway, didn't pay for TV, just used an antenna (still don't have regular cable, just Netflix and HBO Now), kept the house hotter in summer and colder in winter (up to 85 in the summer and down to 60 in the winter - put plastic on the windows in the winter too). My dad bought my first desktop from Circuit City when they went out of business so I could do homework at home instead of going to their house all the time - it was '07 when I got it and internet for the first time. There were points in my life where I was paying tuition and renting and raising a child, so I picked up habits like unplugging everything not in use, which I still do today but not to the extent that I did when I REALLY needed to save - I would even unplug the oven when I wasn't using it. Now I just have everything in surge protectors and shut those off and unplug when that room isn't in use.

I'd just shop at Aldi (we still do, for a family of 3 we spend around $150 a month - but I also started growing a lot of food this year), car was paid for so basic insurance and maintenance = little cost and I walked to work as much as I could (I have a trick knee that likes to sublux/dislocate on occasion). My son is 16 now, and he drives that car but he had to work off $600 worth of chores to get to drive it and call it his (insurance company said rates would be lower if the title was still in my name until he's 18). I had to have internet because I was also in school as an online student, so I got the cheapest deal for that service, and I splurged on Netflix. Took out Pell Grants but it didn't cover tuition and had to pay that too, which sucked but whatever. I'd write it off on my taxes, get a bigger refund, and use that to pay for next semester/year. I guess the Pell grants count as help. Didn't buy much junk food, just what we needed, didn't buy myself any clothes (last minimum wage job was a total joke call center place, no dress code so I didn't have to worry about professional attire). Cell phone service was through ting.com, which charges you for what you use, a minimum $6 service charge. The only reason I don't have them now is because it's no longer worth the savings to not have a retail store to go to/insurance plan. I think my cell bill then was like $18 a month when I used it a lot.

My fiance moved in with me some time when I was working at shitty call center. I charged him for 1/3 of shared bills because I was already paying for my son and myself, didn't want him thinking I was looking for someone to support us or that I'd get lazy. I sporadically get child support, maybe $700-1,000 a year, so there's more help! If I didn't need it for anything, it went into my son's savings. So, he contributed to 1/3 of mortgage payment, utilities and groceries after he moved in with me, but he didn't start contributing until I had been working with that pay for a year. That saved me about $250-300 a month which I put in savings for emergencies, after paying for the higher utility and grocery bills bc another person was living with us. I think over that last year he was living with us, we had to call out a washing machine repair man, a fridge repair man, and the ceiling caved in in our dining room - had to have the chimney flashing put back on correctly and the guys who did that also reinforced the roof through the attic - that was $700, which is amazingly cheap. Fiance and I repaired the dining room ceiling ourselves and put in a new light. I also used part of the savings to put a fence in so our dogs could roam the yard without being on a chain.

It's very tough to do live on minimum wage, but it's doable. Other than the call center, every job I've had that started at minimum wage gave raises, usually after 90 days. I constantly had to budget, like every month look at variable costs and figure out where to save more money. Anything extra went towards my son's care - he needed clothes more than I did because he was growing - I'm an adult so there's no need to buy clothes unless what I have is in absolute disrepair, hair cuts, physicals. Most of my adult life I hadn't made more than $15k a year (including EIC from tax refund), aside from my 1st year of work, and my dad would help with child care. My brother and his wife helped out with that after dad died, but charged me $65 a week, which was still a deal. When I lived out of state in Dallas, my friends would help out by picking my son up from school if I had to work late until I could afford daycare.

I've had to live in one bedroom apartments with son o'mine, when he was really little and the closet was big enough in the bedroom, that would be his "bedroom". When he was 5, he got the bedroom and I got a futon in the living room. My first place I moved into was a 2-bedroom and I had a roommate; I was also a manager at my job and making good money, but my son and I shared a room (he was almost year old when we moved in).

I had MC+ for my son when he was born - automatically qualified because I had him at 16, and we've been on Foodstamps twice, each for 6 months. Once when I was saving up to buy a house, I think it was like a year before I bought the current house, and another time a couple of years ago when I had to have knee surgery and was out of work for a few months. I was out of work twice in 2 years, once was work comp issue that wasn't properly diagnosed (was paid 2/3 of regular income - 2/3 of $7.25/hour), the other was bad knee coming back from work comp injury and being out of work. First time was June to November, second time was the following April to October, so I think the latter time was when I had to get foodstamps.

I probably could have gotten section 8 housing, foodstamps indefinitely, medicaid, free lunch for the kid at school, whatever other benefits/welfare stuff these last 16 years, but I already felt bad enough getting Pell grants (and student loans the first time around - big mistake) for school and getting free help from my dad. I also didn't want to become dependent on government aid, and certainly didn't want my son growing up thinking it was totally normal and ok to live off of those benefits most of one's life.

We make a lot more money now, I think a combined $60k or so at minimum (hard to say bc fiance gets bonuses and I own my business, so it's whatever the profits are = my pay), but our total budget including: mortgage, groceries, full coverage car insurance, new car payment, home maintenance, clothing, utilities, internet entertainment, pet care, phone, etc., is still $2500 per month. So we budget for roughly 2 gross full-time federal minimum wage incomes and the rest goes towards our early retirement/debt snowball (state minimum wage is $7.65 here). And we can have a new car, go out occasionally, take vacations. I don't understand how people can't do this on minimum wage, especially when many states are higher than federal level.

TL;DR:When I hear people bitch about not having money, it's usually because they can't plan and budget or make sacrifices to get what they really want. This opinion of mine is based on dealing with co-workers at different low-wage jobs, the majority of them unable to take care of themselves. I even have a friend who makes $20k/year, no dependents or pets, no car payment, takes out student loans, lives in income-based housing and STILL can barely make ends meet. Rent also goes up. The lowest rents are what is the most money that can be charged to the poorest people while still leaving them enough money to just barely scrape by. When the poorest people have more disposable income. their landlords look to increase rent to the new maximum that they can charge to keep them in the same standard of living of just barely getting by.

By what about rent controls, surely that can stop the rates from going up too much? Nope. Most landlords realize that they can put some money into their buildings (new windows, carpets, flooring, furnaces, roof, etc) and that if they can show actual expenses to the rent control board, then they can (usuallu) increase the rent beyond the maximum 2% or whatever they're allowed to increase each year. They will gladly borrow money if needed because the tenant pays for the loans through their rent, and the interest is a tax deductible expense, then they get to raise the rent 2% or whatever next year from this new higher rent.

Now the other rental properties that are nicer, in better neighbourhoods and generally go for higher rent, well their owners see that some "slum" is now renting for a price that is now a lot closer to what their "nicer" building rents for. Now they are losing money in their minds, so time to up the rents.

The stores that lower income people shop at are mostly run by people making a similar wage. Well, now the owner of those stores has to pay their employees more, and where does that money come from? Raise the cost of goods or eat the cost. We know which choice HAS to be made in this instance (fuck Wal-Mart though, they could easily afford to pay their people a living wage but they care more about their shareholders than they do their own employees who run the stores and make their revenue possible....they have signs in the back of every store that says the customer is #1, the shareholder is #2 and the associate is #3).

Also, where someone was making $5 something an hour, they would have been in the lowest tax bracket and paid damn near nothing in tax. Now, they're going up several brackets and where I live, now they will be in the 25% bracket. So yes, they got a raise, but now they have to pay taxes they didn't have to pay before, pay more for rent, pay more for everything else they buy and have less money in their pockets after the same expenses. So that wage increase did nothing to make their lives better, now they just have to spend more of their money to be in the same place they already were.

The real cost of this is the erosion of the middle class. All of their costs go up too, so they have less money to spend, without the benefit of an income increase. A strong middle class spending money is what drives our economies. Not as many people as the middle class, by far, and the middle class spends WAY more money on consumer goods than the rich do (100 people spending $1,000 is a lot more than one rich person spending $10,000 on a nicer version of X).

The solution to poverty is not forcing people to pay poor people more, they will still have a poverty mindset. Poor people need education and the ability to make better choices. Until they have that, they will always be poor.
